item.title: Deceived With Kindness
item.description: This book wasn’t a Trafalgar Street Book Club (TSBC) choice, but I read it, in a roundabout way, because of the club. Simon Peters had chosen Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway for our September meeting and as an additional bonus we decided to have our first TSBC outing, spending a Saturday touring both Virginia Woolf’s Monk’s House in Rodmell and her sister, and fellow Bloomsbury matriarch, Vanessa Bell’s house, Charleston. It was on the tour of Charleston that the guide in Vanessa Bell’s bedroom told us the story of Angelica, Bell’s daughter by Duncan Grant, who’d married one of Grant’s ex-lovers, David Garnett, 26 years her senior. Garnett had apparently said at Angelica’s birth, “I think of marrying it. When she is 20, I shall be 46 – will it be scandalous?” The guide also told us that Angelica had written an autobiography. As I was curious about the story, and the Bloomsbury group in general, I thought it would be an excellent addition to my interwar reading list. In mid-September I took a two-day solo holiday to Cambridge to look around the town and visit the Duxford Imperial War Museum. I went by train and read most of the book on the journey there and back, finishing it off during a couple of evenings later in the month.

item.title: Orwell
item.description: This book was a recent purchase, bought only a couple of weeks before reading. After being deep in Orwell-land for the last month, I felt I had to read a biography. This was recommended in various places as one of the best. I knew nothing of D.J. Taylor before ordering this book, but he is apparently a well-respected journalist, novelist, and writer. He’s a self-confessed Orwell obsessive, coming back repeatedly to the same subject. This book is a 2019 rewrite of his original 2003 biography. Several new collections of correspondence, particularly between Orwell and various girlfriends, have come to light in the intervening years, shedding new light on Orwell the man, and particularly his romantic life.
